title: Systematic Sampling
breadcrumb: Sampling theory → Systematic sampling → Random start, inclusion probabilities and variance
engineName: Choose a random start and select every kth unit from an ordered frame.
objectives: Construct a linear systematic sample from an ordered frame.
Calculate first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
Explain the restricted sample space compared with SRSWOR.
Calculate exact design variance by enumerating possible starts.

prereq.name: Sampling frame and population size
prereq.why: The interval is calculated from the ordered frame size.

prereq.name: Inclusion probabilities and variance
prereq.why: Joint inclusion probabilities determine design properties.

traps: The random start is selected from 1,…,k in the standard linear design.
Equal first-order inclusion probabilities do not imply the same variance as SRS.
Only k systematic samples are possible when N=nk.
Many second-order inclusion probabilities are zero.
A periodic frame pattern aligned with k can be harmful.
A single sample generally cannot provide an unbiased design-based variance estimate.
howto: Compute k=N/n, choose the random start from the first k positions and add k repeatedly. Each unit is included under one of k starts. Two distinct units occur together only if they occupy the same residue class modulo k. For exact variance, enumerate all k possible sample means.

scenes.title: The frame, interval and random start
scenes.objective: Refresh ordered frames and equal-probability selection.
body: Systematic sampling selects units from an ordered list using a fixed interval. The frame contains N units and the design selects n units, often with N=nk.
A random start r is selected from 1,…,k. The sample is r,r+k,r+2k,…,r+(n−1)k. Every unit has the same first-order inclusion probability in this design.
The ordering matters. If the frame contains a periodic pattern related to the study variable, systematic sampling can produce an unusually high or low sample.

items.recall: The list or operational representation from which units are selected.
refresh: Systematic sampling moves through this ordered list at a fixed interval.
Coverage errors arise if the frame omits eligible units or includes ineligible ones.

items.ask: What is the interval k when N is divisible by n?
refresh: N is the frame size and n is the required sample size.
Divide N by n to obtain the spacing between successive selections.
The standard equal-interval design uses an integer k.

items.recall: Randomising the first position gives each eligible unit a known selection chance.
refresh: The first position is chosen randomly from 1,…,k.
All later selections follow the fixed interval.
Without a random start, this is not the stated probability design.

ask.q: Once the random start is chosen, how are the remaining units selected?
ask.nudge: Add the fixed interval k repeatedly.

scenes.title: A simple route through an ordered list
scenes.objective: Explain systematic selection and periodicity risk.
body: Imagine a register of 20 households and a required sample of four. The interval is five. A random start from positions 1 to 5 determines one of five possible samples.
If the start is 3, select positions 3, 8, 13 and 18. Every possible start gives four observations and every household appears in exactly one of the five possible samples.
This design is operationally simple and spreads the sample across the list. However, a repeating pattern with period five can align with the interval and make the selected units unrepresentative.

scenario.teaser: A register ordered by street blocks
scenario.title: When the order helps or harms
body: A municipal register contains 2,000 households and the survey selects 200, so the systematic interval is ten. The list is ordered geographically, which can spread interviews across the municipality with little fieldwork complexity. If household characteristics vary smoothly along the ordering, the spread may be useful. But suppose every tenth entry is a corner shop and the survey is intended to estimate household electricity use. Depending on the random start, the sample could repeatedly select corner shops or avoid them. This periodic alignment is a risk created by the relationship between the frame order and the fixed interval, not by unequal first-order inclusion probabilities.
Before using systematic sampling, inspect the frame order and consider whether periodicity or hidden grouping can coincide with the interval.
scenario.q: What is the main risk in the corner-shop example?
scenario.answer: Periodicity: the frame pattern may align with the sampling interval.

ask.q: Does equal first-order inclusion probability guarantee that every possible sample is equally likely?
ask.nudge: No. The design only permits the k samples generated by the k possible starts.

scenes.title: Explore the possible starts
scenes.objective: Enumerate systematic samples for a small frame.

viz.caption: For N=20 and k=5, the random start has five equally likely values.

body: For N=20 and n=4, k=5. Start 1 selects 1,6,11,16; start 2 selects 2,7,12,17; and so on.
There are five possible samples, each with probability 1/5. Each population unit occurs in exactly one of these samples, so π_i=1/5.
Only five of the many possible size-four subsets can be selected. This is why pairwise inclusion probabilities are zero for most pairs.

ask.q: What is the probability that unit 14 is selected?
ask.nudge: It is selected only when the random start is 4, so the probability is 1/5.

blocks.body: Assume N=nk and choose r uniformly from {1,…,k}. The selected positions are r,r+k,…,r+(n−1)k.
π_i=1/k=n/N for every unit i. Each unit is selected for exactly one of the k possible random starts.
For distinct units i and j, π_ij=1/k if i and j are congruent modulo k; otherwise π_ij=0 in this linear design.
For a population-mean estimator, each possible start gives a systematic sample mean ȳ_r. V(ȳ_sys)=(1/k)Σ_{r=1}^k(ȳ_r−Ȳ)^2. The total estimator variance is N² times this quantity.

A single realised systematic sample reveals only one of the k possible start-specific means. Since many pairs have π_ij=0, the usual pairwise-probability unbiased variance estimator is unavailable for those pairs. A single systematic sample therefore does not generally permit an unbiased design-based variance estimate without additional assumptions or design features.

flow.title: Systematic selection
flow.alt: Calculate interval, choose a random start between one and k, select every kth unit, then inspect the frame order for periodicity.
flow.note: The random start determines the random component in the basic linear design.

ask.q: Why are many π_ij equal to zero?
ask.nudge: Only units at the same residue position modulo k can appear together.

scenes.title: Worked sample and inclusion probabilities
scenes.objective: Construct a sample and calculate its probabilities.
scenes.problem: A frame has N=20 units and n=4. The random start is r=3. List selected positions and calculate π_i.

steps.why: The interval determines spacing between selected positions.

steps.say: Start at three and add five repeatedly.
steps.why: The sample contains four positions separated by the fixed interval.
There are five equally likely starts.
Every unit belongs to exactly one of the five possible samples.

ask.q: What is π_8,13 for this design?
ask.nudge: The positions differ by five and occur together for start three, so π_8,13=1/5.

scenes.title: Retrieve the systematic rules
scenes.objective: Recall interval, start and inclusion probabilities.
scenes.intro: Try each prompt before revealing the answer.

items.a: k=N/n, when N is divisible by n.

items.q: When is π_ij=1/k for distinct units?
items.a: When the two positions are congruent modulo k in the stated linear design.

items.q: Why can variance estimation be difficult?
items.a: Many pairwise inclusion probabilities are zero and only one start is observed.

scenes.title: Complete a systematic sample
scenes.problem: A frame contains N=36 units and n=6 are required. The random start is r=4. Complete the selection.

steps.why: The interval is the frame size divided by the sample size.

steps.say: Begin at r=4 and add six repeatedly.

blank.hint: Start at four and keep adding six.

steps.why: Every frame unit is selected by one of six equally likely starts.

ask.q: What is the probability that unit 35 is selected?
ask.nudge: It is 1/6, as for every unit in this design.

scenes.title: Systematic sampling versus SRS
scenes.objective: Compare sample spaces and variance implications.

blocks.body: SRSWOR permits every subset of size n with equal probability. Linear systematic sampling with N=nk permits only k possible samples, one for each random start.
Both designs can have π_i=n/N. Equal first-order probabilities do not imply equal second-order probabilities or equal variance.
The exact design variance is the variation among the k possible start-specific estimates. Its value depends on how y-values are arranged in the ordered frame.

blocks.h: When systematic sampling can work well
blocks.body: A well-ordered frame can spread the sample across the population. A periodic pattern aligned with k can be harmful. Randomising or carefully ordering the frame can reduce this risk.

ask.q: Why can two designs with the same π_i have different variances?
ask.nudge: Their joint inclusion probabilities and sets of possible samples differ.

scenes.title: Guided practice: diagnose periodicity
scenes.objective: Identify alignment between a frame pattern and interval.
scenes.problem: A factory register is ordered by production line, with every sixth entry belonging to the night shift. A systematic sample uses k=6. Explain the risk and suggest a safeguard.
hints: Consider what each possible start selects.
scenes.answer: The period six pattern is aligned with k=6. Each start repeatedly selects the same position within the six-entry cycle, so the sample can overrepresent or miss a shift category. Randomise the frame order or stratify by shift.
scenes.check: The periodicity period equals the systematic interval.

scenario.title: The interval matches a repeating shift pattern
body: A factory register lists machines in a repeating order: five day-shift machines followed by one night-shift machine. The survey selects every sixth machine using an interval of six. Depending on the random start, the sample can select only night-shift machines or only day-shift machines. The first-order inclusion probability of each machine remains 1/6, but the sample space is restricted to six possible samples and each sample is highly homogeneous with respect to shift. This illustrates why equal inclusion probabilities alone do not protect against periodicity.
A better approach may randomise the list or stratify by shift and sample within each shift, depending on the survey objective and frame quality.
scenario.q: What frame feature creates the risk?
scenario.answer: A repeating period equal to the systematic interval.

solution.say: Identify the repeating period: six positions.
Compare it with the interval k=6.
A random start selects the same position in each repeated block.
Randomise the frame or stratify by shift.

ask.q: Would changing the random start alone remove the structural risk?
ask.nudge: No. It changes which repeated position is selected, but each sample remains aligned with the cycle.

scenes.title: Avoid systematic-sampling traps
scenes.objective: Distinguish probabilities, sample space and variance.

items.claim: For N=nk and a uniform random start, every unit has π_i=1/k.
items.why: Each unit is selected for exactly one of the k possible starts.

items.claim: Systematic sampling permits every size-n subset with equal probability.
items.why: Only the k interval-spaced samples generated by possible starts can occur.

items.claim: Equal first-order inclusion probabilities imply equal variance under systematic sampling and SRS.
items.why: Second-order probabilities and sample spaces differ.

items.claim: In the linear design, distinct units in different residue classes modulo k have π_ij=0.
items.why: They cannot be included together under one random start.

items.claim: A periodic frame pattern aligned with k can be harmful.
items.why: The sample may repeatedly select the same phase of the pattern.

items.claim: One realised sample generally reveals all possible start-specific means.
items.why: It reveals only the mean corresponding to the realised start.

scenes.title: Transfer: variance across possible starts
scenes.objective: Calculate exact design variance by enumerating starts.
scenes.problem: A frame of N=8 units has n=2 and k=4. The four possible systematic sample means are 3, 5, 7 and 9. Calculate the population mean and design variance of the sample mean.
hints: Average the four possible sample means.
Calculate squared deviations from that mean.
scenes.check: The mean of the four start-specific means is six and the mean squared deviation is five.

solution.why: The design expectation averages equally over four starts.
These are deviations of the possible systematic sample means.
The variance averages squared deviations over the random-start sample space.

ask.q: Why can this exact variance not usually be calculated from one realised sample?
ask.nudge: The other three start-specific means are not observed.

scenes.title: Systematic sampling checklist
body: For N=nk, calculate k=N/n, choose r∈{1,…,k}, and select r,r+k,…,r+(n−1)k.
Every unit has π_i=1/k=n/N. In the linear design, distinct units in different residue classes modulo k have π_ij=0.
The exact design variance is the variation among the k possible start-specific estimates. It depends on the arrangement of values in the ordered frame.
Only one start is observed in a single sample. The usual pairwise-probability unbiased variance estimator is generally unavailable when many π_ij are zero.
Inspect the frame for periodicity aligned with k. Equal first-order probabilities do not guarantee low variance.

ask.q: Which estimator and key design condition should you remember for Systematic Sampling?
ask.nudge: State the estimator, its weighting or expansion rule, and the assumptions behind its variance.

scenes.title: Mastery check
scenes.objective: Demonstrate independent command of systematic sampling.

sheet: π_ij=1/k for same residue class; zero otherwise.
Periodicity aligned with k can be harmful.
tricks: List k possible starts before computing pair probabilities.
Check whether i−j is a multiple of k.
shortcuts: A pair in different residue classes cannot appear together.
Exact design variance is variance across possible starts.
remember: Systematic sample space is smaller than SRS sample space.
One start does not reveal other start-specific estimates.
